doc.title: Tom Albert and Milton "Mooney" Martin Interview, 1964-12-21

chapter: Trombonists, old string bands and dance steps
title: Buddy Johnson versus Yank Johnson as trombonists; Frankie Duson
summary: Martin ranks Buddy Johnson, the 'Papa Trombone', as one of the best trombonists in New Orleans, a reader who could also boot it up. Tom says Yank was the better ragtime player, and Martin remembers Yank as very loud. Frankie Duson could play anything but could not read.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: I used to have some better. I was going to ask some more about the trombone, the two brothers, Yank and Buddy. Which was the better trombone, do you think, Mooney? Which would you rather hear? If you had your choice to hear, was one of them better than the other? I was about to say.
I'd say, Buddy was one of the best trombone jails in New Orleans ever for. Buddy. Used to call him the Papa Trombone. Really, really?
Yeah. One of the very best.
You see, he could read that music and then he could get in there and boot them up. Yeah. See?
Yanky was a better ragtime player. You understand? He was better for ragtime.
How did Yank sound, did he?
Oh, Yanky. Yanky was a tough trombone player. He was tough. You could stand near and eat at Cornhole Street and say, oh, that was Yanky.

Yeah. He could play. Yanky was a tough trombone player. Him and Yanky and, did that have music? Yanky and, oh, you gon' remember that? Chuck? No. Deucin? Deucin. Frankie Deucin. Oh, that's Deucin. Yeah. Yeah. Then them fellas, you see, could, anything the reader would play, they could play it. Yeah. He's had a good ear, I guess. Yeah. Anything the reader could play, they could play it. Yeah. That's our buddy of Frankie Deucin stayed in that WPA band. He ain't know he couldn't read. Well, he could fake, so.
He ain't know he couldn't read.
